blocks.x: Young and Lua, not much. Okay, it's... That is necessary anyway.
No, that's all right.

I'll ask where you were born. You can give your name first, if you wish. Oh, don't you know where I was born? In order to identify it, so that we lose the box to the tape and start playing the tape, we'll have your name on there. Oh. Oh.
What do you want?
You want me to start now? It's all right, it's short. You can just give your name.
Say this is Lua, huh? Am I close enough?
Yeah, that's fine.
You don't... Ah.
You won't even have to lean forward.
Oh, I see. This is Lillian Hardin Armstrong speaking. Well, how is that Hardin? H-A-R-D-I-N.
That's my maiden name. And where did you come from?
Memphis, Tennessee.
You were born there?
Born in Memphis, Tennessee, yeah.
And you say you're a little younger than Louie.
A little, a little bit.
Well, he's not old, is he?
Yeah.
What else now? I wondered about when you first took up music. Studied music? Yes. And the first music you heard, were anybody, any other members of the family musical?

Oh, they say that my father played the mandolin, but he died when I was three years old, so I don't remember him. Oh, I see. And, oh, I, we had an organ in the front room, as they called it there. The left room. We had an old organ, and, oh, ever since I was large enough to reach it, I was trying to play it, so I used to have my cousin peddle it while I'd sit up on the stool and try to play, oh, such a terrible noise. So then I would pretend the windowsill was a piano in Oregon and play that. So when I started the school, my mother decided that she'd better give me music lessons. So I took lessons from a, from a, from the third grade teacher. She taught, she wasn't my third grade teacher, but she taught third grade in the public school, and she taught music also. Her name was Miss, uh, Violet White. So she started me taking lessons. And then, uh, later I took, uh, from, uh, Mrs. Hooks, there in Memphis, who had a Hooks School of Music. And, uh, when I was about 11 years old, she had a graduation exercise, and I was supposed to graduate in music, got my little diploma, and flowers, and everything.
What kind of pieces did you play?

That was mostly classical? Yeah, all classical. I never, it's strange that I never had heard any jazz while I was in Memphis. Only once. Or, a little at a time, I should say. I had a cousin that used, that had a guitar. When I was too small to, um, realize what he was playing, but he used to play the guitar, and he sang, uh, what the people, uh, from New Orleans called Buddy Bolden Blues. But at that time, he called it some, very nasty.
Yeah,
I know. And my, my aunt used to, fuss at him all the time, until he was, uh, no good, he'd never be worth anything, long as he played, uh, shall I call the name of the song?
That's all right.
As long as he played funky butt on the guitar.
Yeah, they even,
but I didn't know, I didn't know,
they print that all the time.

So that's the only blues, or jazz I heard, I remember hearing while I was a child. Because, uh, I played all the marches at school, and I played for Sunday school, all the hymns, and my little classical pieces, by Gregg, and, and, and, McDowell, and things like that. And then, uh, when I went to Fisk, I, I was a music special there. And, after graduating from the school in Memphis, they put me in a second grade music, when I went to Fisk.
That's in Nashville, is it?
Yes. They claimed that, um, I had talent, but I had been poorly taught.
I know a lot of teachers are that way. I could,

yes, I could read anything they'd put up, but, I hadn't been taught technique, so they started me all over again, on scales, and using my fingers, uh, correctly. Well, I went to Fisk, two and a half years, and my mother moved to Chicago.
So, when did you get here?

Oh, it was, um, well, we moved here the last part of, uh, 1918. And, um, I was to go back to school the following, uh, September. In the meantime, I went down State Street one day, and I passed this music store, with all this music in the window, so I went in and asked the lady for a song, that I had heard, but I didn't know the name of it, so I hummed it over, and, uh, they had a man there, playing, demonstrating music, and he said, oh, I know what it is, so, he played it, oh, for me, but he didn't play it so well, so I said, let me play it. And, uh, he said, okay, so I played it, and he said, oh, you can play, and he said, you want a job demonstrating music? I said, oh, I don't know, I said, I just want to buy this piece of music, so he said, well, come back at three o'clock this afternoon, and see the boss, so I went back to three o'clock that afternoon, and, uh, when I walked in, the lady said, miss, his name was Frank, so he said, Mrs. Jones was the lady, his name who owned the stores, was Jones Music's store, so she said, oh, Frank, this is nothing but a child. He said, but I don't care, she can play, he said, play something for us, so I, so he put a couple of pieces of sheet music on the piano, and I played them for, and she said, oh, well, all right, she said, honey, if you want to work, I'll give you three dollars a week, well, I didn't worry about the three dollars a week, all I wanted to do was to learn all the music, without having to buy it, so I went home, told my mother, I had a job playing this music store, for three dollars a week, so she said, no, indeed, you have not, you will not work for three dollars a week, I said, oh, I just want to learn all the music, I said, they got a, oh, the counters and counters, full of music, and I can learn it, you don't have to buy it, and she said, well, all right, if that's all you want to do, so I started right away to memorize all the pieces, because I didn't know how long I'd be there, well, after the, two or three days, everybody that came in the store, they would stand around the piano, and, and listen to me play, I had learned all the music, and I'd be getting to add some extra things to it, and then I was playing my little classical pieces, you know, so I became the talk of the neighborhood, little girl down the music store playing, and about the third week, oh, yes, the second week I was there, she raised me five dollars, she gave me eight dollars, because the people had began to come in and listen, and, so, well, I'm talking pretty fast, huh, too fast? No,
that's true, no, I was watching, I was watching the volume meter, oh, I see, mm-hmm, I watched the volume meter occasionally,

so, well, I imagine about the, after I'd been there about a month, this band from New Orleans came in the store one day, and this woman booked musicians and singers, in different cabarets, and, and, dance halls, too, so, they came in there, to see this woman about getting a job for her, and that was this band from New Orleans, with Eddie Garland, Roy Palmer, Lawrence Dewey, Sugar Johnny, and, who's playing drums? Tubby Hall, I guess.
I was going to say one of the hall boys.

Yeah, Tubby Hall, Tubby Hall, and I see who else was there, oh, and Jimmy Pillai. Oh, on violin. On violin, but they didn't have a piano, they didn't use a piano, so, Mrs. Jones booked them at a Chinese restaurant on the west side. I can't find anybody to tell me the name of that restaurant, of where it was, do you remember?
I don't remember if Ed Garland might have told us, or I've seen Lawrence Dewey, He told me he didn't remember. Well, maybe, maybe Lawrence Dewey might remember.

Well, it was, anyway, it was a Chinese restaurant, because every night they used to give them steaks, and they, the boys used to eat steaks, you know, and they tried out all the piano players around. Mrs. Jones sent them all the men piano players, none of them suited them. So, one night she decided to send me over. So, I went over with the band, and, I asked for the music. So, Eddie Garland was the one who called the numbers, and Lawrence Dewey was the one who used to knock them off, you see. So, I said, where's the music? They said, we haven't got any music. I said, what key are you in? They didn't know what key it was in. He said, when you, when you hear two knocks, just start playing. So, I said, all right. So, they said, boom, boom, and I just hit everything. I just made a bang on the piano. I just hit it. I said, well, whatever key they're in, I'll be in it. I banged on the piano, so it only took a second for me to feel. Which key they were in. What key they was in, and, and at that time, you know, most of the numbers that they play only had three or four changes in it anyway, so, you know, one, you know them all. So, after the first piece, they said, oh, listen to that little girl. And they said, you want to stay with us? So, I said, I don't know. So, they said, well, how much you make at the music store? So, I said, I make $8 a week. They said, you stay with us, you get $27.50 a week. I thought, I thought they were joking. I said, oh, no, you won't either. They said, oh, yes, we will. So, I said, well, I'm not so sure I can stay. I don't think my mother will let me work in the cabaret. And so, they said, well, if anybody asks how old you are, you just tell me you're 21. So, I said, all right. So, I was afraid to tell my mother because I knew she wouldn't let me work there. And they said, don't go back to the music store. Then I was afraid not to go back to the music store. I was afraid Mrs. Jones would call my mother and tell her. So, anyway, I took a chance. I didn't go back to the music store, but Mrs. Jones didn't tell on me. So, we stayed at this Chinese restaurant, I imagine about four weeks. And then they got an offer to come on the south side to the deluxe.
Oh, yeah.
Deluxe Cafe. So, I was still getting this $27.50 a week, but I was only taking the $8 home.
Oh, you're a man.

I didn't dare tell her. I didn't dare. She knew it was something wrong. So, I was saving it, putting it in a book. And, I couldn't, I couldn't wear clothes like the entertainers and other girls because then my mother would get some pictures if I come up with some new clothes. So, I was playing in all these school clothes, these midi blouses.
Didn't she come home pretty late though at night? Yeah,
well, I told her, oh, I told her we were playing at, that's, oh, I'm ahead of myself. I told her I was playing at a dance studio where they taught dancing. Oh, yeah,
sure.
Well, they all, they only played till 12 o'clock.
Mm-hmm.

So, I told her it was a dance studio. Mm-hmm. So, I told her it was a dance studio. Mm-hmm. And, she said, what kind of dance do I say? Where they, where they teach dancing. So, I used to come home and do these, um, soft shoe dances and things and show them. I told her that's what they was teaching. Well, that was dances that I had learned in Fisk from the girls who were taking dances. Mm-hmm. So, after I was at the Deluxe, about, I played up there, the West Side and the Deluxe, three months before my mother found out.
Mm-hmm.

And, one day she was on the porch and a lady came by and said, I saw your little girl at the cabaret last night. Oh. She said, my little girl? I said, yeah. I said, I saw her playing at the cabaret last night. And, my mother said, well, I, I don't know. She said, well, all right. And, when the lady left, she says to me, what were you doing playing at a cabaret last night? So, I said, oh, the, the studio gave an exhibition and I had to play for them. Ha! Said, oh, just one exhibition? I said, yes. So, that went by. The next week, another lady came by and said, I saw your little girl at the cabaret last night. Mama said, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, oh, I want the truth. Something's going on wrong. And so, I started crying. Because I knew, I knew she'd make me quit. So, she said, what's the matter with you? What are you crying about? I said, it is a cabaret and I'm playing there and I'm getting $27.50 a week. And, oh, her mouth opens away. $27.50 a week? I never heard of such salary, she said. I said, I went and got all the money out of the book and brought it and showed it to. Oh, well, she was exasperated with me and she was disappointed. She was everything. She said, to think how hard I worked to make you a lady and you end up in a stinking, nasty cabaret. She said, you'll quit tonight. You will not go back. So, I cried again. So, she said, I said, well, if I quit, they'll make me pay a $100 fine. She didn't like that. So, she said, well, I'll send Mr. Miller up there with you. That was my stepfather. So, she sent Mr. Miller to investigate this dump I'm playing in. So, he came in, sat down, he looked all around. He looked all around. So, he went back and told it was a regular sporting house.
Oh,

gosh. He went back and told it was a sporting house that they were doing everything up there. So, my mother came back. She dressed and came back up there. And while he was gone, I explained to the boss, Mr. Shaw, that my mother had found out I was working up there and that she was coming to start some trouble. And he said, don't worry, don't worry, I'll fix everything. So, when she came in, I went by, he said, you give me a sign when she gets to the door. So, when she came to the door, I gave him a sign, you know, he read at the door. Oh, I bet you're Lillian's mother. So, she, I said, she says, yes. And I came to investigate. She says, you know, Lillian's not of age. And he said, oh, she's such a nice and such a smart little girl. I said, now you just listen to all the people, how they applaud for when she finished. And I could see my mother's chest.
And I said, she was getting proud of me.

Well, when he got through talking with us, she decided that I could stay. But she would come after me every night. So, I was the hot Miss Lill till about 12 o'clock. And then she'd be standing at the door. You know, this was upstairs. So, I was, I was embarrassed to have my mother standing there waiting for me. So, I told her, I said, wait downstairs. Don't come upstairs. And though she got, then she got tired of coming up there. And she says, she met the band. And she decided that Tubby Hall would be all right to bring me home. So, Tubby had the job of bringing me home. Tubby used to bring me home every night. So, what else do I want to know? That's about the first thing. You want to know about those people?
Did Bichet ever come up at that time?

Yes. Well, after, after we were there, I don't know. I don't know exactly how long. But anyway, while we were at the Deluxe, Bichet came in town with a show. I think it was that Mary somebody's show. Mary Mack.
Oh, Mack. Yes.
I interviewed them today,
by the way. I was just over there.
I think that was the show. Anyway, he came in town with a show, and I don't know whether they broke up or what. Anyway, he joined our band, so we had two clan legs in the band.
At the Deluxe.
At the Deluxe. And everything went all right until they got the paychecks mixed up one night. Dewey and Bichet. And Bichet found out Dewey was getting more than he was. He quit.
Oh.
So, let's see who else came up there. Oh, and after we were up there a while, I don't know exactly how long, we went across the street to Dreamland.
Dreamland. The same band with Dewey and Sugar Johnny and all.

No. Sugar Johnny was taking care while we were there. And Freddie Kepler took his place. Freddie Kepler. Freddie Kepler took his place. Now, I don't remember who was with him when we went across the street. Dreamland. Anyway, we went across that and didn't stay very long. I'm trying to think. I don't know where else would happen. What else did we know?
I wondered about when you joined Oliver's band.

Oh, well, Eddie Garland, oh yeah, Eddie Garland, the boys, oh, Dewey went back to New Orleans. And anyway, the band broke up while we were at Dreamland. I don't know for what reason. The band broke up, but I stayed on as a pianist and every band came, I worked with them. So, a clarinet player, a violin player, I mean, Jimmy Corral? Walsh, I think he called him. Oh. Walsh had a band there after that and I stayed and played piano with them. And it was while I was at Dreamland that Oliver came to the gardens. And when he came to the garden, he asked me to come over to the garden and play with him. Oh, no, no, I mean, no, that's not right. Oliver came to the Dreamland to work. And I stayed at the Dreamland and worked with him. With him,
right there.

Then while we were there, we got an offer to go to San Francisco. So, we went to San Francisco in May 1921. Not May, well, it was the spring of 1921. Yeah, it was pretty much. We went to San Francisco and worked at the Pergola Ballroom on Market Street. You know that? Yes. Well,
what should I tell you? Well, it's interesting to hear that I didn't know just how you joined the band where you were.
Yeah, I joined the band at Dreamland. And, oh,
there's one thing.
Oh, did we go there before?
Somebody told me once there was a lady out there whom I knew once. Even made some records with her in Bunk Johnson. Bertha Gonsolin.
Well, that's afterwards. I'll get to there.
I wonder,
some people said
she made the Jeanette records,
came back east with you. No, no, no, no.
That you left the band
and she took a band over. She didn't make any Jeanette records.
She didn't know.

No, no. We went to this ballroom in San Francisco and stayed six months. Then, we went across to Oakland and played at the cabaret for about two or three weeks. I don't remember the cabaret, but it was in Oakland. Then, after that, after that job closed, they decided to go to Los Angeles. Well, I was afraid to keep staying out there because I slipped off to go there anyway. I told my mother we were going somewhere to make a record. See, anyway, when she heard from me, I was in San Francisco. So, after that, I came back to Chicago and I went back in Dreamland to work. That's when I worked with this woman's band, May Brady, when I came back. That was, well, the beginning of 22, see? And Joe stayed out there and he and Eddie Garland and the whole band. Oh, yeah, and incidentally, Minor Hall joined the band somewhere because he went to San Francisco with us.
Oh, yeah.

Yes. He was with us in the Dreamland and he went to San Francisco with us and then he quit out there and they sent for Baby Docs. Baby Docs joining us out there. Yeah, Baby Docs joining us out there. So, they stayed out there another year and that's when Gonzalez came back. She came back to a... Oh, wait,
Gonzalan, Bertha Gonzalan.
Yeah, she came back to Chicago with the band.
She did come back with them.
She came back from Los Angeles with them. Yes. I think they worked at the Garden. Yes, they worked at the Garden when they came back and I was still at the Dreamland. I was never straight
on that part about Bertha
whether she really played. Yes, she came back.
She didn't make the records.

No, we hadn't made the records yet. Now, this is 22. This is 22. So, she went back to Los Angeles. When she went back to Los Angeles, I joined Lenore. Well, now, let's see. Louis came to join Oliver while I was still at Dreamland because the first night he was in town, Oliver brought him over to Dreamland to meet me.
It was not at the Royal Garden then, it was at the Dreamland.
That he met me.
Met you.
I was playing there, but he was playing with Joe at the Gardens.
That's right.
You weren't with him.
See,

I wasn't with him. That's right. Then Joe asked me to join the band again and this girl went back. So, I joined the band. Then that made Louie and all of us the same band. And it was after I joined the band again and Louie was there that we made the records which was 23.
Yes.
The spring of 23. That's straight.
That's straight. That's all straight. All right. Now,
she had gone back to Los Angeles when we made the records. Yes. That's what I thought. She didn't stay here too long.
But I wasn't sure she ever came each.

Yes, she came here because I left the band in Frisco and they went to Los Angeles so they had to have somebody replace me. She replaced me in California. And when they came back, she came back with them. But I don't know whether she didn't like you. I don't know why she didn't stay.

I saw Bertha and knew her very well in 1943. Did she say anything? She seems to be dead now. I don't remember what she told me exactly. She didn't make those Bertha. We didn't make any interviews you see on tape and I didn't talk to her very much about them.
I definitely went to Richmond. I have it in a book in my mother's writing. She wrote Lillian Left for Richmond. I think it's April 23. She's got the exact tape down there. So Bertha
seems I couldn't find her at all. I'm afraid she's dead now.
Oh, yes, she was. She was with the band and that had to be 22.

Yes. I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about the band that made those records for Columbia, the New Orleans Wonders that you used with Mitchell because I asked George Mitchell about the date and he didn't even remember some of the other people.
You don't remember the... Oh.
He couldn't...
Well, now I'm gonna...
That's what it had
for me and Dodd, so... I'd like to get this point straight about this New Orleans Wonders. Tommy Rockwell asked me to get a record date together with musicians
Yes.

and to have... and to make six numbers and to have Louis compose three of them and I compose three. Get this straight. So, I wrote all six of the numbers. So, I put Louis' name on three and myself on three as composer.
Notice his name is on the label as composer. Wait a minute. So,
I got $120 for making the records. I remember I was at $112 something like that. Anyway, when I got the money for making the records I gave half to Louis and I kept half.
Was he with Henderson in New York then?
No! He's here in Chicago. Oh, no, no.
How come he wasn't on the date then?

He didn't want Louis. He told me purposely he didn't want Louis on the date because Louis was signed up with OK. OK, I see. You see? Louis couldn't be on the date but he wanted Louis to write three of the numbers. I didn't know at the time why. So, when the records come out the numbers that Louis composed his name is written on there in big letters as though he was playing on it.
Yeah, I think he was on the date.

So, Louis and I had a big argument. Louis slapped me about it. He said that I knew about it but I didn't know. All I know he told me to have him write three. Do I know what they're going to put on the label? No. Oh, yes. That's the only time Louis obstructed me. He slapped me and he said I had no business making the records that he told me nothing. He had already spent half of the money that I gave.
Oh, boy. That was a big mess.
Well, that's exactly the way that happened. Now, you know, it's very unusual for a composer's name to be written as large as they were on that nuance. It must have been some reason for it. Yeah.
They thought they'd sell better.

Well, I was the one got the blame. So I chose well, I got the band together and that was the first time that we had ever made a recording session where the parts were written out. I wrote out every part for that for Peter's. It was all written
out.

Oh, yeah. I wrote it out because we'd always been playing the same thing. Everybody take a window, you know, and play what they want to play. So I said, on this piece I'm going to have something to play. And after that all the different band-lees and things were calling me up to make arrangements. I said, I don't know how to make arrangements. Well, I hadn't studied arranging then and I was afraid to take the job making arrangements. They said, but you had the clarinet doing something while the other part was doing something. I said, oh, well, that was just an idea. You know, where I wrote it for them, I didn't want to get involved in writing for other bands. But I did write some trio
courses for. Quite a few solos, I remember.
Just the choruses alone.
Did you write out the solos like for Johnny Dobbs or when St. Cyr took a little banjo solo?
Well, Padida Street was everything written out. I told him how I wanted everything played on that piece.
That's the greatest one.
That's the one I made. That's the one I wrote.
That's great.
And I told him how I want. I told Johnny I wanted to make the first solo high and the second in the low register.
That's a great note.
And then the banjo came in after the introduction. And Mitchell was supposed to make the introduction. The banjo came, dunk, dunk, dunk. That was all my brainchild. Mitchell
couldn't even remember who was on that date. I reminded him it was Ori and there was no drums. Was it Ori? It's Ori and
St. Cyr and
Mitchell.
But I know we rehearsed right here in this room. Right here we had rehearsed. Right here. Just one
rehearsal for
that date? That's all. Well, as a rule, we'd never rehearsed before. We'd never rehearsed before we'd make a record date. We'd do it in the hot and rehearse
sometimes.
I don't remember rehearsing. We rehearsed in the studio.
Mitchell was saying Jelly Roll used to rehearse quite a bit for his records sometimes. Two or three. Just one rehearsal for that.
Well, sometimes when we recorded with singers, we would rehearse the singers. We rehearse one singer
with

Bud Scott and Johnny and that bunch. This later, I don't know, I can't remember her name, but we were rehearsing and she was singing and so she stopped and she said, I can't sing that song on that temperature. She broke up the record and said, oh, the band fell out, laughed, you know, and she was looking me straight in the face and I couldn't laugh. she still doesn't know what to say. Bud Scott said, well, what temperature would you like?
What?
She heard somebody say tempo, I guess. I can't sing that song, temperature.

What are we going to ask? One more thing and I won't bother you anymore. About Freddie Kepard, of course, Louis Kepard, his brother is still living down there. But Freddie Kepard, I never did know him personally and I never heard him in person except the few records he made.

Well, I told you he played a short time of Deluxe with us when Sugar Johnny was taking L. And then I doubled with Freddie Kepard out of Lorraine Gardens. That was, must have been 40th and stayed out that way somewhere. That was an after-hour place. I played with him there. I think he was a very fine trumpet player.
Did you compare with all of her? Personally,

oh, you don't put me on the side. Personally, I think he was a better trumpet player. But, of course, Oliver had his style and he, you know, everything we played was organized so well under Oliver. You noticed all the numbers we played? Everybody would know what they were supposed to do. Forever,
were those numbers ever written out? No,
no, but we
rehearsed. They rehearsed.

And we knew there was no fumbling around for the introduction or the ending. We knew what we were going to end. It started with how we were going to end. And Lou and Oliver knew when they were going to make their solos. It was a well-organized band.
But Freddie

Kepard, I don't know, when I worked with him out to the Lorraine Garden, it was just five or six pieces and nothing was arranged, we just played. But he could really blow a trumpet. And he had a nice, clear, strong tone. I can
tell that from the record. But they say he was better in person.
Too bad he didn't make more recordings. And he was a, well, he was kind of a jolly, carefree sort of person.
Did he work at the Dreamland with you too?
Not with me. In later
years?
No, I worked with him only at the Deluxe
Deluxe
and the Slow Rain Garden. And now he worked with Charlie Cooper, somebody on the west side.
Jimmy Noon.

Yeah, on the west side. But I didn't work with him any place else. So when Louis was working at the Dreamland with Ollie Powers Band, that's after he'd left Oliver, everybody started talking about Louis playing because it was the first time he'd been able to be heard alone, you see. So Freddie heard about people talking about Louis one night. No, Louis was working with me that time. It wasn't Ollie Powers. I had the band there for a short time. That's after he left Fletcher Hennessey. That's what I thought. You got the I.M.
there.

Freddie Keppett came in one night and stood by the band standing. He said, when Louis got through playing, he said, let me have your horn, boy. Louis looked at me, and I bired my on the band stand. He stood outside and he blew and he blew and he blew. And so everybody applauded him. Then when he got through and he gave Louis back the horn, I said, get him. He
stayed there. He didn't walk out.
No, he didn't get him. I went to Louis now,
you get
him. Oh, you have never heard such playing in your life. Because he was angry. You never heard him play bang, bang,
bang.
And when he got through playing, people were standing up on the chairs cheering. I
had been there that night.
Freddie eased out. He challenged him, all right. Asked him for his own horn.
Yeah. That's really a good story. I don't want to bother you longer, but I certainly appreciated hearing about these old times from New Orleans. ! Too bad I'm
not
from New
Orleans. Well there's more New Orleans musicians up here at that time than down there almost. Oh
I suppose so because
of the
deluxe wheel. Manuel Perez came and played. You remembered him
too.
Yes Manuel Perez he came and played a little while.
I thought that was earlier. I didn't know he was here at

segments.title: Recording setup, name and birthplace in Memphis
segments.summary: Mic check, she gives her name and maiden name and says she was born in Memphis, a little younger than Louis.

segments.title: Family music, first lessons with Violet White and Mrs. Hooks
segments.summary: Her father played mandolin; she played the family organ, took lessons from Violet White and Mrs. Hooks and graduated in music at about 11.

segments.title: Hearing Buddy Bolden Blues from a cousin in Memphis
segments.summary: Her only childhood exposure to jazz was a cousin singing a version of Buddy Bolden Blues on guitar; otherwise she played classical pieces, marches and hymns.

segments.title: Studying at Fisk and the move to Chicago
segments.summary: At Fisk she was told she had talent but poor technique and was started over on scales; her mother then moved to Chicago.

segments.title: Demonstrating sheet music at Jones Music Store
segments.summary: Soon after arriving in Chicago in 1918 she got a job playing songs at a State Street music store, learning the stock and drawing crowds.

segments.title: Joining the New Orleans band at a Chinese restaurant
segments.summary: A New Orleans band (Garland, Palmer, Dewey, Sugar Johnny, Tubby Hall) tried her out, and she joined at $27.50 a week without telling her mother.

segments.title: Hiding the Deluxe job and pay from her mother
segments.summary: At the Deluxe she keeps taking home only $8, saves the rest, and tells her mother she plays at a dance studio.

segments.title: Mother discovers the cabaret job and investigates
segments.summary: Neighbors tell her mother; her stepfather reports it a sporting house, but the boss charms her mother into letting Lil stay if Tubby Hall brings her home.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet joins the Deluxe band
segments.summary: Bechet joined the band after arriving with a show and quit when a pay mix-up showed Dewey earned more.

segments.title: Moving to Dreamland and Freddie Keppard replacing Sugar Johnny
segments.summary: The band crosses the street to Dreamland, with Freddie Keppard taking Sugar Johnny's place.

segments.title: Band breaks up; joining Oliver at Dreamland
segments.summary: The band broke up at Dreamland; she stayed as house pianist, then worked with Oliver when he came to Dreamland, and they got an offer for San Francisco.

segments.title: San Francisco, Oakland and the Bertha Gonsoulin question
segments.summary: They worked at the Pergola Ballroom in San Francisco for six months, then Oakland; she clarifies that Bertha Gonsoulin replaced her but made no records, and she returned to Chicago in early 1922.

segments.title: Bertha's return and Louis Armstrong meeting her at Dreamland
segments.summary: Sorting out Bertha Gonsoulin's comings and goings, and how Louis, newly in town with Oliver, met Lil at Dreamland.

segments.title: Rejoining Oliver's band and the 1923 records; Bertha's timeline
segments.summary: She rejoined Oliver so she and Louis were in the same band, which made the spring 1923 records; further discussion of when Bertha was in the band.

segments.title: Organizing the Columbia date and the composer credit dispute
segments.summary: She assembled the New Orleans Wonders date, wrote all six numbers, split the pay with Louis, and the oversized composer credit led to an argument in which Louis slapped her.

segments.title: Written parts and arrangement on Perdido Street
segments.summary: It was the first session with written parts; she wrote out Perdido Street in detail, directing solos for Johnny Dodds and the banjo intro, and was later asked to arrange for other bands.

segments.title: Rehearsing for record dates and a singer's 'temperature'
segments.summary: Who was on the date, the single rehearsal, rehearsing singers, and a funny story of a singer who mistook tempo for temperature.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard's playing compared with Oliver's organized band
segments.summary: She played with Keppard at the Deluxe and Lorraine Gardens, thought him a fine trumpeter, and contrasts the unarranged work with Oliver's well-organized band.

segments.title: Keppard challenges Louis at the Dreamland
segments.summary: Where else she worked with Keppard, then the story of Keppard borrowing Louis's horn and Louis outplaying him.

segments.title: New Orleans musicians in Chicago: Perez, Tio, Dixon
segments.summary: Many New Orleans players were in Chicago; she recalls Manuel Perez and Tio at the Deluxe and a drummer and banjoist with Franz Jackson.

segments.title: Tony Jackson and the Deluxe entertainers
segments.summary: Tony Jackson played for the girl singers at the Deluxe and doubled at the Pekin before he fell ill and died.

segments.title: Hearing Jelly Roll Morton and her loud supporting piano style
segments.summary: Hearing Jelly Roll Morton made her play hard; the New Orleans men preferred her supportive playing and Oliver objected to her getting fancy.
